title: How to Make Coffee Filter Ghosts: Easy Kids Craft
h1: How to Make Coffee Filter Ghosts: Easy Kids Craft
description: Learn how to make coffee filter ghosts: an easy, low-cost Halloween craft for kids, plus ideas for ghost garlands, glowing ghosts and window decorations.
author: Just Halloween Crafts
body:
Coffee filter ghosts are a classic Halloween craft for a good reason: they cost almost nothing, they take only minutes, and children of nearly every age can make them. With a few round paper filters, some cotton wool and a black marker, you can create a whole crowd of friendly little spooks to hang in windows, string into a garland or float above a party table.

This guide shows you how to make a basic coffee filter ghost step by step and then shares several ways to take the idea further, from glowing ghosts to colorful watercolor spirits.

Supplies for Coffee Filter Ghosts

  • White basket-style (round, fluted) coffee filters
  • Cotton wool balls, scrunched tissue or a small foam ball for the head
  • White string, thread or thin elastic bands
  • Black permanent marker or felt-tip pen
  • Scissors
  • Optional: liquid starch or a mix of white glue and water, watercolor paints, googly eyes, fishing line, LED tea lights

Basket filters give the best ghostly ruffle. Cone-shaped filters can be used too if you trim them into a rough circle first.

How to Make a Coffee Filter Ghost: Step by Step

Step 1: Make the Head

Roll two or three cotton wool balls together, or scrunch a piece of tissue, into a ball about the size of a large marble. This will form the ghost's head. For bigger ghosts, use a small foam ball or several layers of tissue.

Step 2: Cover the Head

Flatten one coffee filter and place the cotton ball in the center. Gather the filter down around the ball so it is fully covered and the edges hang down like a sheet. For a fuller ghost, use two filters stacked together.

Step 3: Tie the Neck

Wrap a piece of string or a small elastic band around the filter just below the ball and tie it firmly. This shapes the head and lets the rest of the filter flare out like a flowing robe. If you want to hang the ghost, leave a long tail of string or thread a loop through the top of the head with a needle.

Step 4: Draw the Face

Use a black marker to draw two eyes and a mouth. Round "O" mouths look surprised, wavy lines look spooky and big smiles look friendly. Press lightly, as the marker can bleed into the paper. Googly eyes are a fun alternative for younger children.

Step 5: Shape the Robe

Gently pull and fluff the edges of the filter so the ghost looks as if it is drifting. You can snip small notches around the hem for a tattered look.

Optional: Stiffen Your Ghost

For a ghost that stands up on its own, dip the shaped filter in liquid starch or a mix of equal parts white glue and water. Drape it over a small bottle or jar topped with the cotton ball head and leave it to dry overnight. Once dry and stiff, lift it off and add the face.

Creative Coffee Filter Ghost Ideas

Ghost Garland

Make eight to ten ghosts and tie them at intervals along a length of string or ribbon. Hang the garland across a fireplace, doorway or window. Mix them with paper bats or our easy tissue paper garland for a fuller look.

Floating Window Ghosts

Tie each ghost to a length of clear fishing line and hang them at different heights from a curtain rail. They twist gently in the air and look as though they are floating, especially when the window is lit from inside.

Glowing Ghosts

Drape a stiffened ghost over a battery-powered LED tea light. The paper diffuses the light into a soft, eerie glow that looks lovely on a windowsill or party table. Always use LED lights rather than candles with paper crafts.

Watercolor Spirits

Before assembling, let children paint the flat filters with watercolors in purple, green and orange, or drip on diluted food coloring. Coffee filters soak up color beautifully and create tie-dye patterns. Once dry, make them into ghosts for a bright, playful twist.

Ghost Treat Toppers

Instead of a cotton ball, place the filter over a round lollipop and tie it at the neck. Draw on a face and you have instant party favors. Keep these for older children, and remember that some guests may have food allergies.

Ghost Mobile

Cross two sticks or wooden dowels and tie them at the center, then hang ghosts from each end with thread of different lengths. Balance the mobile by sliding the ghosts along the sticks until it hangs level.

Tips for Making Coffee Filter Ghosts with Kids

  • Pre-cut the string into lengths before you start, so little hands do not have to wait for scissors.
  • Help with tying: younger children can hold the head in place while an adult ties the neck.
  • Use washable markers for very young crafters, and cover the table in case of bleed-through.
  • Keep small parts away from under-threes: googly eyes and cotton balls can be a choking hazard.
  • Make it a group activity: coffee filter ghosts work brilliantly for classrooms, clubs and parties because the supplies are cheap and the results are quick. See our guide to hosting a Halloween craft party for kids for planning tips.

Storing Your Ghosts

Coffee filter ghosts are light and fragile, so store them flat in a shallow box between layers of tissue paper. Stiffened ghosts keep their shape better if you store them upright in an egg carton. Keep them somewhere dry, as damp will make the paper limp.

Coffee Filter Ghost FAQs

Which coffee filters work best?

Round, fluted basket filters are the easiest to use because they already have a ruffled edge that looks like a flowing sheet. Unbleached brown filters can be used too, and they make great "old, dusty" ghosts for a haunted house theme.

Can I make them without cotton wool?

Yes. A scrunched ball of tissue, newspaper, a small pom pom or even another coffee filter rolled into a ball all work well as the head. For a weightier ghost that hangs straighter, use a small foam ball.

How long do starched ghosts take to dry?

Most stiffened ghosts are dry within 8 to 12 hours in a warm room. Thicker layers of glue mix can take up to a day. Do not try to speed up drying with a hairdryer held close, as it can blow the ghost out of shape.

Can coffee filter ghosts go outside?

They are best kept indoors, as rain and damp will make the paper soggy. For a porch display, hang them in a sheltered spot or inside a window where they can be seen from outside.

More Easy Halloween Crafts

Coffee filter ghosts are proof that the simplest crafts are often the most fun. Once your ghosts are hanging, why not add some paper spider webs, a few pom pom bats or some toilet paper roll Halloween crafts? You will find even more ideas in our collection of Halloween crafts for kids.

title: How to Host a Halloween Craft Party for Kids
h1: How to Host a Halloween Craft Party for Kids
description: How to host a Halloween craft party for kids: planning, easy craft stations, a sample schedule, spooky snacks, safety tips and take-home favors.
author: Just Halloween Crafts
body:
A Halloween craft party is a brilliant alternative, or addition, to trick or treating. Children get to be creative, everyone goes home with something they made, and you avoid the sugar overload of a traditional party. Whether you are planning a small get-together for a few friends or a busy afternoon for a whole class, a little preparation makes all the difference.

This guide covers everything you need to plan and host a Halloween craft party for kids: guest numbers, choosing crafts, setting up stations, a sample schedule, snacks, safety and take-home favors.

Planning Your Craft Party

Guests and Ages

Decide how many children you can comfortably fit around your tables. As a rough guide, plan for one adult helper for every four to six young children, and one for every eight or so older children. Knowing the age range helps you choose crafts that are neither too easy nor too frustrating.

Timing

For children under six, 60 to 90 minutes is plenty. Older children can happily craft for up to two hours with a snack break. Weekend afternoons in the run up to Halloween work well, and early evening is fun if you want the party to finish with glowing decorations.

Space and Budget

Crafting gets messy, so choose a room with wipeable floors or cover carpets with old sheets. Most Halloween crafts can be made from inexpensive or recycled materials, so set a budget early and collect supplies such as cardboard tubes and glass jars for a few weeks beforehand.

Choosing the Crafts

Three or four craft stations is the sweet spot. Mix one or two quick crafts that take ten minutes with one longer project, and include at least one activity that does not need drying time. Here are some ideas that work well at parties:

  • Coffee filter ghosts: quick, cheap and suitable for almost every age.
  • Toilet paper roll characters: bats, mummies and monsters made from recycled tubes.
  • Paper spider webs: fold-and-cut webs that feel like magic when unfolded.
  • Salt dough ornaments: bake the shapes in advance and let guests paint them at the party.
  • No-carve mini pumpkins: decorate with foam stickers, markers or paint.
  • Pom pom bats: best for older children who can wind yarn.
  • Craft kits: ready-made sets save preparation time. See our guides to foam craft kits and mask craft kits.

Make a sample of each craft before the party. It helps you spot tricky steps, work out how much of each supply you need, and gives children an example to copy.

Setting Up Craft Stations

  1. Protect surfaces: cover tables with wipe-clean tablecloths or brown paper, which kids can also doodle on.
  2. One craft per table: put all the supplies for each project together in a tray, with a sample and a simple picture card showing the steps.
  3. Prepare components: pre-cut string, wings, hats and templates so children can focus on the fun parts.
  4. Create a drying zone: set aside a table or tray lined with paper, and label each child's work with their name on masking tape.
  5. Provide aprons: old t-shirts make great paint shirts.
  6. Have wipes and a bin at every table to keep things under control.

Sample Party Schedule (Two Hours)

  • 0:00 to 0:15: arrival, name tags and a simple coloring sheet while everyone arrives.
  • 0:15 to 0:50: first craft stations; groups rotate every 15 to 20 minutes.
  • 0:50 to 1:10: snack break while paint and glue dry.
  • 1:10 to 1:45: remaining stations and finishing touches.
  • 1:45 to 2:00: show-and-tell parade of creations, then pack up take-home bags.

Spooky Snack Ideas

Keep food simple and easy to eat with clean-ish hands. Serve snacks on a separate table away from paint and glue. Some ideas from our Halloween food collection:

  • Eyeball cupcakes or spider cupcakes
  • Chocolate spider webs as edible decorations
  • Savory Halloween appetizers for children who prefer savory food
  • Fruit "pumpkins" made from peeled clementines with a small celery stalk on top

Always ask parents about food allergies and dietary needs before the party, and label any foods containing common allergens such as nuts, dairy, eggs or gluten.

Safety Tips

  • Keep hot glue guns, craft knives and ovens for adults only.
  • Avoid small items such as beads, googly eyes and buttons for children under three, as they are a choking hazard.
  • Choose washable, non-toxic paints and markers.
  • Use LED tea lights rather than candles anywhere near paper decorations.
  • Have a basic first aid kit nearby and know which parent to contact for each child.

Take-Home Favors

The crafts themselves are the best party favors. Give each child a paper bag to decorate as a monster at the start of the party, then use it to carry their creations home. For something extra special, small felt bags made with our pumpkin trick or treat bag pattern can be reused every year.

Clean-Up Made Easy

Ask children to help tidy their station before moving on, roll up paper tablecloths with the scraps inside, and wash brushes straight away before paint dries. Store leftover supplies in a labeled box ready for next Halloween.

Decorating the Party Space

You do not need to spend much on decorations. Hang a few garlands across the room, put out some glowing jars and pumpkins, and add finished crafts to the display as the party goes on. Children love seeing their own ghosts and bats become part of the decorations. A simple themed backdrop made from black paper with paper bats and a moon also makes a great spot for photos at the end.

Halloween Craft Party FAQs

What age is best for a craft party?

Children from about four years old can enjoy a craft party with plenty of adult help, while children aged seven to twelve can work more independently and try more detailed projects. Choose crafts that match the youngest guests and offer extra challenges, such as adding details or making a second piece, for older ones.

How many crafts does each child need to make?

Two to four finished crafts per child is usually plenty for a party of 90 minutes to two hours. More than that can feel rushed, and children enjoy having time to add their own finishing touches.

How can I keep costs down?

Choose crafts made from recycled materials, buy basic supplies such as paint, glue and card in bulk, and ask guests to bring a cardboard tube or glass jar with them. Simple projects like paper webs and coffee filter ghosts cost only a few pennies per child.

Can the party be held outdoors?

Yes, a garden or yard party works well on a dry day, especially for messy painting. Weigh down paper with stones, keep a sheltered area ready for drying crafts, and have an indoor backup plan in case of rain.

Ready to Party?

A Halloween craft party lets children enjoy the season in a creative, hands-on way, and the decorations they make will brighten your home all month. Plan your stations, prepare a few samples, and let the spooky fun begin. You will find many more ideas in our Halloween crafts for kids section and on the blog.

title: How to Make Mason Jar Halloween Lanterns
h1: How to Make Mason Jar Halloween Lanterns
description: How to make mason jar Halloween lanterns step by step: painted jack-o'-lantern jars, mummy jars and tissue paper luminaries lit safely with LED tea lights.
author: Just Halloween Crafts
body:
Mason jar Halloween lanterns are one of the easiest ways to add a warm, spooky glow to a porch, mantel or party table. A few clean glass jars, some paint or tissue paper and a battery tea light are all it takes to turn kitchen recycling into a row of grinning jack-o'-lanterns, wrapped mummies or glowing stained glass luminaries.

This tutorial walks you through one basic method step by step, then shows you five different designs you can make with the same technique. The projects suit adults and older children, and younger kids can join in with the decorating once the jars are prepared.

What You Need to Make Mason Jar Lanterns

You do not need special canning jars for this craft. Any clear glass jar with smooth sides will work, including clean pasta sauce, jam and pickle jars. Wide-mouth jars are easiest because you can reach inside to place the light.

  • Clean, dry glass jars with labels removed
  • Rubbing alcohol or warm soapy water and a lint-free cloth
  • Acrylic craft paint or multi-surface paint in orange, white, black and green
  • Foam brushes or soft flat paintbrushes
  • Black permanent marker or paint pen for faces and details
  • Tissue paper in Halloween colors and a decoupage medium such as Mod Podge (for the luminary design)
  • White cheesecloth, gauze or strips of muslin (for the mummy design)
  • Googly eyes, twine, ribbon and thin craft wire (optional)
  • Battery-operated LED tea lights or a small string of fairy lights

Before You Start: Choose a Safe Light

Paint, paper and fabric decorations can catch fire, so use battery-powered LED tea lights or fairy lights inside your lanterns rather than real candles. LED lights stay cool, can be left on for a whole evening, and are much safer around children, pets and trick-or-treaters' costumes. Many come with a flicker setting that looks surprisingly like a real flame through orange glass.

If you use your jars outdoors, place them on a level step or table where they will not be knocked over, and bring them inside if heavy rain is forecast so the paint and paper stay in good condition.

How to Make a Painted Mason Jar Lantern: Step by Step

The painted jack-o'-lantern jar is the classic version and a good one to make first. Once you are happy with the method, you can adapt the colors and faces for the other designs below.

Step 1: Clean and Prepare the Jars

Soak the jars in warm soapy water to loosen the labels, then scrub away any sticky residue. Dry them thoroughly and wipe the outside with a little rubbing alcohol on a cloth. This removes greasy fingerprints so the paint grips the glass evenly.

Step 2: Paint the First Coat

Paint the outside of the jar with thin, even strokes of orange paint. Work from top to bottom and leave the rim unpainted if you plan to add a ribbon or wire handle later. The first coat will look streaky; that is normal. Let it dry completely, which usually takes 20 to 30 minutes for acrylics.

For a softer glow, try dabbing the paint on with a foam brush or sponge instead of brushing. The tiny gaps in the texture let more light through.

Step 3: Add More Coats

Add a second and, if needed, a third coat until the color is even. Hold the jar up to a window between coats to check the coverage. Remember that a lantern should glow, so stop before the paint becomes completely opaque.

Step 4: Draw the Face

Sketch a jack-o'-lantern face lightly with a pencil, then fill in the eyes, nose and mouth with black paint or a paint pen. Triangle eyes and a zigzag grin are traditional, but you can make each jar a different character: sleepy, surprised, toothy or downright scary.

Step 5: Finish and Light

Once the face is dry, tie green ribbon or twine around the neck of the jar to look like a pumpkin stalk. Pop an LED tea light inside and your first lantern is ready. If your jars will be handled a lot, seal the paint with a clear spray varnish suitable for glass and leave it to cure as directed on the can.

Five More Mason Jar Lantern Ideas for Halloween

1. Mummy Jars

Paint the jar a pale yellow or leave it clear, then wrap strips of cheesecloth or gauze around it, overlapping them at different angles and securing the ends with a dab of glue. Leave a small gap and stick on two googly eyes peeping out. When lit, the light shines through the layers of fabric for a creepy, soft glow.

2. Tissue Paper Stained Glass Luminaries

Tear orange, yellow, purple and green tissue paper into small pieces. Brush decoupage medium onto a section of the jar, press the tissue pieces on and brush another layer over the top. Overlap the colors so the jar is fully covered, then let it dry. Add a black paper bat or cat silhouette on top for a dramatic finish. Our free printable crow silhouettes and butterfly silhouette template make good stencils for this.

3. Ghost Jars

Frost the jar with two or three coats of white paint, sponged on so it stays slightly translucent. Paint two large black oval eyes and an open "Boo!" mouth. A cluster of ghost jars in different sizes looks wonderful lined up along a windowsill.

4. Spider Web Jars

Paint the jar black, then use a fine white paint pen to draw a spider web radiating from one side. Add a small plastic spider or a pom pom spider on the lid. Alternatively, leave the jar clear and stretch fake cobweb around it for an instant haunted look.

5. Witch's Potion Jars

Paint the jar a deep green or purple, add a printed label and tie twine around the neck. Our free Halloween potion bottle labels fit well on smaller jars and turn them into glowing apothecary lanterns for a witch-themed party.

How to Display Your Halloween Lanterns

  • Porch steps: place a jar on each side of every step to light the way for trick-or-treaters.
  • Mantel or shelf: group jars of different heights with mini pumpkins and fake cobweb.
  • Party table: use small jam jars as glowing centerpieces between plates of treats.
  • Hanging lanterns: wrap craft wire twice under the rim of the jar and twist a loop over the top to make a handle, then hang from a sturdy hook or tree branch.

Tips for the Best Results

  • Paint peeling? The glass was probably greasy. Clean it with rubbing alcohol before painting next time, or use a paint made for glass.
  • Too dark when lit? Use fewer coats, sponge the paint on, or leave the face shapes unpainted so light shines through them.
  • Brush strokes showing? Thin coats dry more smoothly than one thick one. A foam brush also helps.
  • Working with kids? Prepare and base-coat the jars in advance, then let children add faces and decorations with paint pens or stickers.

Light Up Your Halloween

Mason jar Halloween lanterns are inexpensive, quick to make and can be stored away and reused every October. Start with a simple painted pumpkin jar, then experiment with mummies, ghosts and stained glass designs until you have a whole glowing collection.

Looking for more ways to decorate? Try our no-carve pumpkin decorating ideas, make tissue paper pom poms to hang above your lanterns, or browse all of our DIY Halloween decorations.

title: No-Carve Pumpkin Decorating Ideas for Halloween
h1: No-Carve Pumpkin Decorating Ideas for Halloween
description: Easy no-carve pumpkin decorating ideas for Halloween: painted faces, decoupage, push pins, yarn and foam monsters. Safe for kids and longer-lasting.
author: Just Halloween Crafts
body:
Carving a jack-o'-lantern is a Halloween tradition, but it is not the only way to decorate a pumpkin. No-carve pumpkin decorating ideas are perfect for young children who are too little to handle knives, for anyone who wants their pumpkins to last longer, and for crafters who simply enjoy painting and embellishing more than scooping.

An uncut pumpkin stays fresh far longer than a carved one because the skin is still sealed. That means you can decorate early in October and still have a great display on the 31st. Below you will find how to choose and prepare your pumpkins, ten creative no-carve ideas, and tips for keeping your designs looking good all month.

Choosing and Preparing Your Pumpkins

Look for pumpkins with firm, smooth skin, no soft patches and a sturdy stalk. Smaller pumpkins and squashes are easier for children to handle, while large ones make a bold statement on the doorstep. Craft stores also sell faux foam pumpkins, which can be decorated in exactly the same way and kept for years.

  1. Wash: wipe the pumpkin with a damp cloth to remove soil, then dry it completely.
  2. Degrease: a quick wipe with a little rubbing alcohol or a vinegar-and-water mix helps paint and glue stick to the waxy skin.
  3. Protect your table: cover the work surface with newspaper or an old tablecloth, especially if you are painting.

10 No-Carve Pumpkin Decorating Ideas

1. Painted Jack-o'-Lantern Faces

Paint a classic triangle-eyed face onto an orange pumpkin with black acrylic paint. You get the familiar look of a carved jack-o'-lantern without any mess. Outline the shapes with a pencil first, then fill them in with two coats of paint.

2. White "Ghost" Pumpkins

Give a pumpkin two coats of white paint, then add big black eyes and a round mouth to turn it into a friendly ghost. Stack a small ghost pumpkin on top of a larger one for a ghostly snowman effect.

3. Chalkboard Pumpkins

Paint the pumpkin with chalkboard paint and let it dry. You can then draw faces, write spooky messages or a "Happy Halloween" greeting with chalk, and change it as often as you like. Children love wiping off the face and starting again.

4. Decoupage Napkin Pumpkins

Separate the printed top layer from a patterned paper napkin, tear it into pieces and smooth them onto the pumpkin with decoupage medium. Bat, spider and damask designs all look effective. Finish with one more coat of medium over the top to seal it.

5. Push Pin Patterns

Press metallic thumbtacks or dome-headed push pins into the skin to create polka dots, spirals, initials or a spider web. This is a great option for older children and adults because it is quick, needs no drying time and looks striking on a mantel. Supervise younger children, as pins are sharp and small.

6. Yarn and Twine Wrapped Pumpkins

Wrap a faux pumpkin in chunky yarn, twine or ribbon, gluing as you go to hold the strands in place. Black and orange stripes look festive, while natural jute twine gives a rustic Fall feel. Add a yarn pom pom on top for a playful finish.

7. Drip-Painted Pumpkins

Place the pumpkin on a jar lid or cup to raise it off the table, then slowly pour slightly thinned acrylic paint over the stalk and let it run down the sides. Try purple and green for a witchy potion look, or layer several colors for a bright, modern design.

8. Craft Foam Monster Pumpkins

Cut eyes, teeth, horns and ears from craft foam sheets and stick them on with glue dots or double-sided tape. This is one of the best no-carve ideas for toddlers and preschoolers because there is no paint to spill. Our guide to Halloween foam craft kits for kids has more ideas for using foam.

9. Witch Pumpkins

Paint a pumpkin green, add a wicked face and top it with a small black witch's hat made from a cone of card glued onto a circle brim. Twist strands of black or purple yarn under the brim for hair. A row of witch pumpkins makes a great display alongside our free "Flying Lessons" witch printable.

10. Spider Web Pumpkins

Paint a pumpkin black and draw a spider web over the top with a white paint pen, starting at the stalk and working downwards. Add a plastic spider, or make one from fused beads using our Perler bead spider web pattern.

How to Make Your Pumpkin Decorations Last

  • Keep them dry: moisture causes paint to peel and pumpkins to rot. Place outdoor pumpkins under a porch roof if possible.
  • Keep them cool: real pumpkins last longest away from radiators, fireplaces and strong afternoon sun.
  • Seal the design: a light coat of clear acrylic sealer helps protect painted and decoupaged designs on display.
  • Check the base: a pumpkin standing in a puddle will soften quickly. Sit it on a cork mat or saucer.
  • Use faux pumpkins for keepsakes: if you want to keep a design for future years, decorate a foam pumpkin instead of a real one.

Display Ideas

Group pumpkins in odd numbers and different sizes for the most natural look. Mix painted pumpkins with plain ones, add dried leaves or straw, and tuck a few mason jar Halloween lanterns among them so the display glows after dark. On a dining table, a line of mini pumpkins painted in a single color scheme makes an elegant centerpiece.

Prefer to Carve After All?

If you decide you want a traditional jack-o'-lantern too, start with our guide on how to hollow out a pumpkin, then try something ambitious like our pumpkin fairy house. Mini pumpkins can even become Halloween dip bowls for your party.

No-Carve Pumpkin FAQs

How long does a painted pumpkin last?

An uncarved real pumpkin kept cool and dry can often last for several weeks, and painting does not shorten that much as long as the skin is not damaged. Carved pumpkins usually last only a few days by comparison.

What paint should I use?

Acrylic craft paint works well on real and faux pumpkins. For pumpkins that will sit outside, look for an outdoor or multi-surface acrylic and finish with a clear sealer.

Can I eat or compost a painted pumpkin?

Do not eat a pumpkin that has been painted, glued or pinned. If you want to compost it, choose plain, unpainted decorations such as removable stickers or ribbon, and take them off first.

Have Fun Decorating

No-carve pumpkins are safer, cleaner and longer-lasting than carved ones, and they give everyone in the family a chance to be creative. Pick one or two of these ideas, gather your paints and embellishments, and enjoy filling your home with pumpkins full of personality. For more inspiration, browse all of our pumpkin crafts.

title: Salt Dough Halloween Ornaments: Recipe and Ideas
h1: Salt Dough Halloween Ornaments: Recipe and Ideas
description: Make salt dough Halloween ornaments with a simple 3-ingredient recipe. Includes baking and air-drying times, painting tips and spooky decoration ideas.
author: Just Halloween Crafts
body:
Salt dough is a wonderful, inexpensive craft material that most families can make from ingredients already in the kitchen cupboard. Rolled out, cut into pumpkins, bats and ghosts, baked hard and painted, it turns into charming salt dough Halloween ornaments you can hang on a Halloween tree, string into a garland or keep as handmade keepsakes for years.

This guide covers a simple salt dough recipe, how to shape and dry your ornaments, how to paint and seal them so they last, and plenty of spooky design ideas.

Basic Salt Dough Recipe

You only need three ingredients. This quantity makes roughly 15 to 25 ornaments, depending on the size of your cutters.

  • 2 cups (about 250 g) plain all-purpose flour
  • 1 cup (about 270 g) fine table salt
  • About 3/4 cup (180 ml) warm water

Tip: fine salt gives a smoother finish than coarse salt. Add the water gradually, as different flours absorb different amounts.

How to Make Salt Dough Ornaments: Step by Step

Step 1: Mix the Dough

Stir the flour and salt together in a large bowl. Add the warm water a little at a time, mixing with a spoon and then your hands, until the dough comes together into a ball. It should feel firm and smooth, like play dough. If it is sticky, add a spoonful of flour; if it crumbles, add a few drops of water.

Step 2: Knead

Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface for five to ten minutes until it is smooth and elastic. Kneading helps prevent cracks later on.

Step 3: Roll and Cut

Roll the dough to an even thickness of about 5 mm (1/4 inch). Thinner ornaments dry faster but break more easily; thicker ones take much longer to dry. Cut out shapes with Halloween cookie cutters such as pumpkins, bats, ghosts, cats, moons and witches' hats. If you do not have cutters, draw a shape on card, lay it on the dough and cut around it with a blunt knife.

Step 4: Make a Hanging Hole

Use a drinking straw or skewer to make a hole near the top of each shape. Make it slightly larger than you think you need, as the dough shrinks a little as it dries.

Step 5: Add Texture (Optional)

Before drying, press details into the dough with a toothpick or fork: pumpkin ridges, cat whiskers, bat wing lines or a stitched mouth on a ghost. You can also stamp letters to make name tags.

Drying Your Ornaments

Salt dough must be completely dry all the way through before you paint it, otherwise it can crack or go moldy later. There are two ways to dry it.

Oven Drying

Place the shapes on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Bake at a low temperature, around 120°C (250°F, or a low gas mark), for about two to three hours for 5 mm thick pieces, turning them over halfway through. Thicker pieces will need longer. The ornaments are ready when they feel hard and sound hollow when tapped. A low temperature is important: too much heat makes salt dough puff up and turn brown.

Air Drying

Lay the ornaments on a wire rack in a warm, dry room and turn them over once or twice a day. Air drying usually takes two to four days, depending on thickness and humidity. This method uses no energy but needs patience.

Painting and Sealing

Once cool and completely dry, paint your ornaments with acrylic craft paints. Paint one side, let it dry, then paint the other side and the edges. Paint pens and fine permanent markers are great for faces and details.

Sealing is the most important step for making ornaments last. Salt draws moisture from the air, so an unsealed ornament can soften over time. Brush on two coats of decoupage medium, clear acrylic varnish or a clear spray sealer, covering every surface including the edges and the inside of the hanging hole.

Spooky Salt Dough Halloween Ornament Ideas

  • Jack-o'-lantern pumpkins: paint them orange with black faces and a green stalk.
  • Handprint ghosts: press a child's hand into the dough, cut around it, and once dried turn it upside down. The fingers become the wavy bottom of a ghost; add two black eyes and a mouth. It makes a lovely keepsake with the child's name and the year on the back.
  • Glittery bats: paint bats black and add a touch of silver glitter to the wings while the varnish is still wet.
  • Candy corn: cut triangles and paint them in yellow, orange and white stripes.
  • Skulls: paint white skulls and decorate them in bright sugar skull colors. Our sugar skull Perler bead pattern is useful for design inspiration.
  • Gift tags: stamp a name into each shape and tie it to a treat bag or party favor.

Ways to Display Them

Hang your ornaments from a bare branch in a vase to create a Halloween tree, thread them along ribbon to make a garland, or tie them to cabinet handles and door knobs. They also look great hung alongside our paper fan decorations or the coffee filter ghosts craft.

Troubleshooting

  • Ornaments puffed up: the oven was too hot. Lower the temperature and dry them for longer.
  • Cracks appeared: the dough was too dry or not kneaded enough, or it dried too quickly. Small cracks can be filled with a paste of flour and water before painting.
  • Soft or bendy ornaments: they are not fully dry. Return them to a low oven or leave them to air dry longer.
  • Paint looks patchy: apply a white base coat first, then add colors on top.

Safety and Storage

Salt dough looks like cookie dough but it is not edible, and the very high salt content can be harmful to pets, so keep dough and finished ornaments out of reach of dogs and cats. Supervise children when using the oven. Store sealed ornaments wrapped in tissue paper in an airtight box with a sachet of silica gel if you have one, and keep them somewhere dry until next Halloween.

Salt Dough FAQs

Can I dry salt dough in the microwave?

Some crafters do, but microwaving often causes bubbles and uneven drying, so oven drying at a low temperature or air drying is more reliable for ornaments you want to keep.

Can I add color to the dough itself?

Yes. Knead in a few drops of food coloring or a little powder paint before rolling. Colored dough is handy for younger children who find painting fiddly, although the colors will look softer once dried.

A Keepsake Craft for Every Year

Salt dough Halloween ornaments are cheap to make, fun for all ages and can be brought out year after year. Try making a few new designs each October and you will soon have a whole collection. For more hands-on projects, explore our hanging Halloween decorations and crafts for kids.

title: Toilet Paper Roll Halloween Crafts for Kids
h1: Toilet Paper Roll Halloween Crafts for Kids
description: Easy toilet paper roll Halloween crafts for kids: bats, mummies, black cats, monsters, owls and glowing eyes, made from cardboard tubes and simple supplies.
author: Just Halloween Crafts
body:
Empty toilet paper rolls are one of the most useful free craft supplies in the house. With a little paint, paper and imagination, a plain cardboard tube can become a bat, a mummy, a black cat or a goofy monster. Toilet paper roll Halloween crafts are ideal for rainy October afternoons, classroom activities and party tables, and they are a fun way to show children how everyday recycling can be turned into something new.

Below you will find how to prepare your tubes, eight easy cardboard tube projects and some tips for getting the best results with children of different ages.

Getting Ready: Tubes and Supplies

Start collecting cardboard tubes a few weeks before Halloween. Kitchen roll tubes can be cut in half to give you two more. Discard any tubes that are damp or damaged, and store the rest somewhere dry.

  • Cardboard tubes from toilet paper or kitchen rolls
  • Acrylic or poster paint in black, white, orange, green and purple
  • Construction paper or card in the same colors
  • White glue, a glue stick and clear tape
  • Scissors (child-safe scissors for younger kids)
  • Googly eyes, pipe cleaners and markers
  • White crepe paper, gauze or toilet paper (for mummies)
  • Optional: glow sticks, string, tissue paper

Paint or wrap? Painting gives a smooth, bold finish but needs drying time. Wrapping tubes in colored paper is quicker and less messy, which makes it a better choice for large groups or very young children.

8 Toilet Paper Roll Halloween Crafts

1. Hanging Bats

Paint a tube black or wrap it in black paper. Fold the top edge of the tube inwards on both sides to make two pointed ears. Cut a pair of scalloped bat wings from black card and glue them to the back. Add googly eyes and a tiny pair of white paper fangs. Thread string through the top to hang your bats upside down from a shelf or curtain pole. For a fluffier bat, see our bat pom pom craft with free wing template.

2. Mummies

Wrap a tube in strips of white crepe paper, gauze or toilet paper, crossing them at angles and securing the ends with glue. Leave a small gap near the top and stick on two googly eyes peeping out. Mummies are perfect for younger children because there is no need for neat edges; the messier the wrapping, the better.

3. Black Cats

Cover a tube in black paper and fold in the top to create ears, just as for the bat. Draw or glue on yellow or green eyes, a pink nose and white whiskers. Cut a long, curly tail from black card and glue it to the back so it curls around the side.

4. Frankenstein's Monster

Paint or wrap the tube green. Glue a strip of black paper around the top with a zigzag edge for the hair. Add googly eyes, draw a stitched scar and a wide mouth, and push two short pieces of pipe cleaner or rolled paper into the sides for the neck bolts.

5. Owls

Fold the top of a brown or purple tube inwards to make ear tufts. Cut two large circles of white paper with smaller black circles on top for the eyes, add an orange triangle beak and glue on paper feathers or wings. Owls look lovely lined up on a windowsill. If your children enjoy owls, they might also like our Perler bead witch owl pattern.

6. Pumpkins

Cut a tube into rings about 2 cm (3/4 inch) wide, paint them orange, then stack five or six rings side by side and tie them together through the middle with green string or a pipe cleaner. The rings fan out into a round pumpkin shape. Add a green paper leaf and a twisted brown paper stalk.

7. Witches

Wrap a tube in green paper for the face and body. Make a pointed hat by rolling a quarter-circle of black card into a cone and gluing it to a black paper circle brim, then fix it to the top of the tube. Glue strands of purple or orange yarn under the brim for hair and draw on a cheeky face.

8. Glowing Eyes in the Bushes

This is a favorite outdoor decoration. Draw pairs of spooky eye shapes on several tubes and cut them out carefully (an adult should do the cutting). Snap a glow stick, drop it into each tube and tuck the tubes among bushes or plant pots at dusk. The glowing eyes peep out of the darkness at trick-or-treaters. Never cut open glow sticks, and keep them away from small children.

Turn Your Tubes into Treat Holders

Cardboard tubes also make great party favors. Fold one end closed, fill the tube with small treats or stickers, then fold the other end and decorate it as a monster or mummy. For a reusable alternative, try sewing our felt pumpkin trick or treat bag.

Tips for Crafting with Kids

  • Prepare in advance: base-coat or pre-wrap tubes the day before so children can go straight to decorating.
  • Choose the right glue: glue sticks are less messy for little ones; white glue holds better for heavier pieces like wings.
  • Adapt for age: toddlers can stick on pre-cut shapes and eyes, while older children can cut wings, draw faces and design their own characters.
  • Watch small parts: googly eyes and pipe cleaner pieces are not suitable for children under three.
  • Allow drying time: painted tubes need about 30 minutes before you add paper pieces, so plan another activity in between.

Display Ideas

Line up your finished characters along a mantel, hang bats from a branch in a vase, or group monsters together as a party table centerpiece. A row of tube mummies and black cats also looks great alongside our coffee filter ghosts.

Toilet Paper Roll Craft FAQs

Are toilet paper tubes clean enough for crafts?

Cardboard tubes from toilet paper and kitchen rolls are generally fine for crafting. Only use tubes that are dry and undamaged, store them in a clean box and ask children to wash their hands after crafting. If you prefer, plain craft tubes can be bought from craft stores instead.

How do I stop the paint soaking in?

Cardboard absorbs paint, so the first coat often looks patchy. Use a thicker acrylic or poster paint, apply a white base coat first, or simply wrap the tube in colored paper instead.

Recycled Fun for the Whole Family

Toilet paper roll Halloween crafts prove that you do not need expensive supplies to create memorable decorations. Save your tubes, choose a few characters and let children's creativity take over. For more simple projects, browse our Halloween crafts for kids and paper crafts.

title: Make Your Own Halloween Fairy Door Craft
h1: Make Your Own Halloween Fairy Door Craft
description: Make your own Halloween fairy door craft: turn a plain wooden fairy door into a witch house with paint and altered art techniques, step by step.
author: M. W. Johnstone
body:
Simple altered art techniques make it easy for you to make your own DIY decorative display items for Halloween. A plain wood fairy door can be transformed in lots of fun ways for this Spook-tacular occasion.

With this make your own Halloween fairy door craft, you can create a wonderfully bewitching item to keep out on display. I show you how I make my own witch themed Halloween fairy door with plenty of photos for your enjoyment.

Be inspired with this fairy door alteration to make your own witch home for Halloween. Or, alternatively, take the process and techniques that are used here to create your own creepy house decoration befitting of October 31st.

Note: This post may contain affiliate links for which I can be compensated.

Make Your Own Halloween Fairy Door Craft

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Make your very own Halloween fairy door decoration that you can display on a mantel, a shelf or a table top. Transforming a plain fairy door into a witch home like the one above is an easy altered art craft that adults and older kids can enjoy.

I chose a witch theme for my design but there are plenty of other themes that you can go with for this seasonal occasion. Use this photo tutorial to gather lots of ideas on how to make your very own Halloween door.

Your altered fairy door blank could be transformed into a haunted house with ghosts and ghouls, a creepy castle, a zombie hideout, a wicked wizard's keep and so much more. Enjoy this Halloween craft tutorial and get inspired.

Fairy | Elf | DIY | Wooden Door |View on EtsyFairy House Pumpkin Door 3D Wooden Elf Shapes Pixie Plywood 3D NEW PMP1View on EtsyFairy Door 3D Opening Wooden Elf House Stone Plain Blank Craft Shapes Pixie Shelf Plywood OFD3View on EtsyMagic Fairy Door open door, Elf Door, Gnome door, doll houseView on Etsy

First, you need your own blank, undecorated fairy door. A wood version is best as it will be more lasting than a cardboard door. Look for one that stands by itself (many are flat and don't) and one that is hinged because it is even more appealing and magical to be able to actually open your door and look through.

You may be able to find fairy door blanks in your local craft store but the best selection I found is at Etsy. Before ordering an undecorated fairy door online, do check that the size is what you want for your chosen display area.

Step 1: Painting the Wooden Fairy Door

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

The first thing I did was to paint my wood door blank. I chose black acrylic paint for the door section and a dark gray acrylic paint for the surround because I knew exactly what look I was going for with the witch theme.

You could just paint the front of your door to save time but I painted all sides so that people can look at it all around on display. I don't advise putting these decorated doors outside as they will not weather too well. Mine is for an indoor Halloween display on a wooden shelf.

There are alternatives to painting. The plain blank wood doesn't really have much of a Halloween vibe so the light wood is best covered. You could use a wood stain, a dark varnish, a decoupage technique where you glue paper on top. Acrylic paint is simple to use and dries quite quickly so that's why I chose it.

Step 2: Adding a Spiderweb Window Detail

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Some fairy door blanks come with a window detail already on the door. Some are etched in place, made with plywood pieces or your window may even be cutout so you can see right through it. Mine did not have one so here's how I made my own.

Since I own a Sizzix Big Shot die cutting machine, it was very easy to cut a circle of silver card out with my circle framelit dies at Amazon.com and also at Amazon.co.uk. You could also hand-cut a circle using a round object as a guide or choose another shape to cut for a window piece. A circle worked best in my instance.

I then die cut a spiderweb from dark gray glitter card which makes a good contrast over the top of the silver circle when you glue it in place. Regular white glue with a thin nozzle applicator works fine.

I also added some frayed white tissue paper on top of the silver mirror card and underneath the spiderweb die cut. You can see this better a few photos down. This added detail makes the door window look like it has clouded up with age from a distance.

You can draw on a cobweb detail instead if you do not have a die cutting machine or cannot cut your own spiderweb small enough.

I'm using the small spiderweb die from the Spooky Halloween Sizzix Thinlits die set. I got mine from Amazon.co.uk. This is a great little set of dies for Halloween and especially good for making cards, scrapbooks and small decorations.

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

After sticking the window detail to the Halloween fairy door, I added in a surround to stop the window look like it is just floating. Using some thick string (wool, twine are perfect) I glued this around the circular window - not too neatly as this is a witch's house.

The string can be glued down using a regular white glue that should dry clear when done. Hot glue can leave messy blobs if you are not careful with it.

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

You can see that just by painting over the top of the string with a medium brown acrylic paint gives it a look of twisted wood surrounding the cobweb window area. It makes a nice detail and fits with the overall witch theme that I'm going for.

Think about the details that you want to add to your own Halloween fairy door to make it truly unique and your own - not just a carbon copy of someone else's design. The details do make for a better display item and one that your guests can enjoy looking at during October.

Step 3: Decorating the Fairy Halloween Door Surround

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

I could have made the fairy door surround look as though it was brickwork or large cobbled stone that would fit with the witch theme. However I knew I was planning to add some detailed die cuts on top including flourishes and these look better on a plain backdrop.

Die cut pieces were used to make all of these elements including the Boo text, the decorative flourishes and flowers. I stuck to a limited color palette of black, purple, silver and gray to fit the scheme.

You can use stickers, paint, rhinestones, fabric and paper flowers and leaves and paper decorations to decorate all around your Halloween altered art door. If you don't have a die cutting machine, look at different scrapbook elements and even paper Halloween sets that you can use to cut decorative items from and easily glue into place.

Step 4: Making a Witch Broomstick to Park Outside Your Door

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

As soon as I knew I was going with a witch theme for my DIY Halloween fairy door, I knew I had to have a broomstick parked outside.

A miniature broomstick is easy to make using a piece of thin wooden dowel rod or a cocktail stick depending on the size of your fairy door. You will also need some embroidery floss in brown for the smallest broomsticks or some wool for larger ones and some twine.

First paint or color the wooden dowel rod which has been cut to a realistic looking size for the fairy door - a broomstick that is way taller than the door section will look weird. I used acrylic paint which I built up in different shades of brown to give an aged look to the broomstick. You can also use a marker pen to color it in.

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Once the colored wood dowel is dry, cut lots of pieces of twine to a length that would work for the broomstick bristles. These pieces should not be cut to exactly the same size as it will look unnatural for a witch's broomstick. Cut them to slightly different lengths.

Use a length of the brown embroidery floss or wool to tie the twine pieces around the bottom of the colored dowel rod. You can also use a hot glue gun or quick dry glue to fasten the twine pieces in place before tying the floss on. This gives you a basic broomstick.

Finished Witch House Halloween Fairy Door Design

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Continue to decorate your Halloween door as you like. I glued the broomstick on to the side with a large black ribbon bow over the top. I added in some paper flowers, a die cut fence and some rhinestones.

I used related objects with the door once on display giving it a backdrop of a haunted forest coloring page, a cauldron made from die cuts, a potion bottle filled with glitter and a ceramic cat. I love how the finished piece came out just in time for Halloween!

title: How to Make a Spider Web Halloween Banner
h1: How to Make a Spider Web Halloween Banner
description: How to make a spider web Halloween banner using cutting dies, spiderweb doilies or paper webs, for spooky cobweb decorations that hang well.
author: M. W. Johnstone
body:
Spiders are always a popular theme for Halloween. You can make a quick and easy spider web banner using a cutting die, spiderweb doilies, or even by making paper webs by hand. These spooky cobweb designs are easy to hang thanks to their natural pattern holes.

Trick or Treat! Enjoy learning how to make a spider web banner which looks very effective as part of your Halloween decorations. Once you have the webs, which can easily be made from die cuts and even doilies, add a fun phrase across the middles using alphabet dies or stickers.

Many kids enjoy making paper spiderwebs as a Halloween paper craft. If they can make at least 3 then you'll have enough to spell out BOO to make a small but cute spiderweb garland.

Note: This post may contain affiliate links for which I can be compensated.

How to Make a Spider Web Halloween Banner Decoration with a Favorite Spooky Saying

A spiderweb banner is a simple but very effective design that is just perfect for adding to your Halloween decorations. I made mine from white and silver papers to look more like the real thing but they also look great made in black and gray.

For more of a family friendly and fun vibe, why not make the spiderwebs from bright Halloween shades such as pumpkin orange, monster green, cosmic purple and blood red. I love to add fun phrases across the middle and then string onto silver cord to finish the design.

Materials and Tools to Make a Spider Web Halloween Banner

Some paper for the spiderwebs or use spider web doilies
A contrasting color of paper to cut alphabet dies or use alphabet stickers
Some cord or twine for hanging up
Dies and die cutting machine if cutting shapes

Step 1: What You Need to Make a Spiderweb Banner

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

There are plenty of ways to make spiderwebs or, alternatively, buy some ready made doilies that are already shaped and cut for you. My favorite way to make spiderwebs from paper is to cut them out using my die cutting machine. That way, I can choose exactly what color I want and quickly cut as many as I need.

I'm using the small spiderweb die from the spooky Halloween Sizzix die set at Amazon.com to make a mini garland. You can also get this Sizzix die set from Amazon.co.uk. This is a great little set of dies for Halloween and especially good for making cards, scrapbooks and small decorations.

There are lots of larger spiderweb dies you could choose from if you want more of a statement banner. Kids can also make their own spiderwebs from paper. You only need 3 of these to spell out the word BOO too.

Because I'm spelling out "Trick or Treat" across my spiderweb banner, I've got an alphabet die to cut all the letters I need. You can just as easily use alphabet stickers.

Step 2: Making the Spider Webs from a Cutting Die

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

I cut out enough spider webs to spell the phrase "Trick or Treat" making sure I also had spider webs to position between the words as well. Since Trick or Treat was a longer phrase, it worked well having the smaller dies.

A small web die would also work well for spelling out Happy Halloween, 31st October and Witching Hour. Smaller phrases include Boo, Spooky and Eeek!

I wanted white and silver card for to look more like real spiderwebs when hanging up. You could choose from other popular Halloween colors such as black, bright green, orange and purple.

Step 3: Adding on Your Chosen Halloween Phrase

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

I die cut my Trick or Treat phrase from black card to contrast with the white color paper webs. You can use alphabet die cuts or stickers to spell out whatever Halloween phrase you like across the middle of your webs.

Small die cut letters can be fiddly to glue into place. Because mine were very small, I used a Quickie Glue pen. You can also use a white or liquid glue with a fine tip nozzle.

Step 4: String Up Your Spider Web Halloween Banner

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

The natural holes and gaps in each paper spiderweb makes it very easy to pass some cord or twine through. Most banners and garlands need you to punch holes in each flag piece so this is much easier.

I threaded each piece onto some silver cord ready to hang up.

The Finished Spider Web Halloween Garland Design

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

I'm really happy with how this delicate looking spiderweb banner design turned out. It finished off my decorations perfectly. I had mine strung across my display cabinet. You may have yours across a wall or suspended from a ceiling.

Simple but effective decorations are often the best. What will you make this Halloween to decorate your home with?

title: Chocolate Orange Cupcakes: Halloween Treats
h1: Chocolate Orange Cupcakes: Halloween Treats
description: Chocolate orange cupcakes for Halloween: zesty orange buttercream on rich chocolate cupcakes, in classic Fall colors for party treats.
author: M. W. Johnstone
body:
Chocolate orange cupcakes are sweet and zesty at the same time. They have a classic flavour combination with the chocolate cupcake base and delicious citrus orange buttercream frosting.

These chocolate orange cupcakes are the perfect treat for Halloween and Thanksgiving with their beautiful Fall and autumnal colors. It is a taste that is hard to beat with the melt-in-the-mouth chocolate cake and smooth yet tangy frosting. A divine pairing of flavors.

Discover how you can bake these delicious chocolate cupcakes with orange buttercream frosting for Fall, Halloween or anytime you want to. For added indulgence, add a couple of slices of Terry's Chocolate Orange on top.

Note: This post may contain affiliate links for which I can be compensated.

Chocolate Orange Cupcakes: Classy Fall and Halloween Treats

Image Credit: Overlay of text added to original photo shared by F_A on Flickr with a CC License

Can you resist cupcakes that look so heavenly? These cupcakes make beautiful party pieces, gifts and sweet bites for Fall, Halloween and Thanksgiving with their glorious shades of rich brown and warm orange. They also taste divine too.

Chocolate and orange are one of the most delightful flavor combinations and not to be missed. Give these cupcakes a try and you'll be rewarded with the perfect blend of sweet and sour as the chocolate and the tangy citrus orange buttercream melt in your mouth.

A List of What you Need to Make These Chocolate Orange Cupcakes

1) Chocolate cupcakes ready to decorate > cupcake recipe on allrecipes

2) Some orange buttercream frosting > frosting recipe on myrecipes

3) Icing or frosting set (optional)

4) Chocolate shavings, curls or sprinkles

5) Fall or Halloween themed orange wrappers

You don't need the Terry's Chocolate Orange as suggested but that is a classic example of just how successfully chocolate and orange work together as a flavor pairing. An English delicacy not to be missed. Try putting a few slices on top of each cupcake for decoration.

How to Make Chocolate Orange Cupcakes for Halloween and Fall

Step 1: Purchase or make up a batch of chocolate cupcakes. Here's a recipe if you don't already have one you like to use >> Chocolate Cupcakes Recipe

Step 2: Let the cupcakes cool down completely on a wire rack before you attempt to add your orange buttercream topping. If you add the buttercream frosting when the cupcakes are still warm, it will start to melt and run off the cakes.

Step 3: While the cupcakes are cooling, make your orange buttercream frosting >> Orange Buttercream Recipe. If you want a strong orange color for the frosting, then you'll need to add in some orange food coloring.

Step 4: Pipe the orange buttercream onto your cupcakes. There is a video on icing swirls on cupcakes below.

Alternatively, spread a very generous amount of buttercream over the top with a blunt knife or spatula which is what I normally do.

Step 5: Using your fingertips, drop some chocolate shavings or chocolate sprinkles on to the orange buttercream icing.

You can buy packs of chocolate sprinkles but I prefer to grate my own chocolate bars to use as decoration on cakes.

Alternatively, try putting a few slices of Terry's Chocolate Orange on top of each cupcake for decoration. This has the wonderful taste of chocolate orange and will match your finished cupcakes to perfection.

Step 6: An orange cupcake wrapper will finish off your chocolate orange cupcakes to perfection. Mmmm, enjoy!

How to Ice Swirls on Your Chocolate Orange Cupcakes

If you want a bit of a fruity tang this Fall season then chocolate orange will be a perfect flavor for your cupcake treats.

title: How to Make a Perler Bead Spider Web Pattern
h1: How to Make a Perler Bead Spider Web Pattern
description: How to make a Perler bead spider web pattern with fused beads, to hang up as Halloween decor or use as unique cupcake toppers.
author: M. W. Johnstone
body:
See how you can make a Perler bead spider web pattern using fused beads. The finished craft is perfect for hanging up as Halloween decor and also to use as unique toppers for Halloween cupcakes too.

Kids and adults can have a ton of fun with Halloween crafting by making some fun, spooky spider webs from fused beads such as Perler and Hama. This how to page has step by step images to show how you can easily make this creepy cobweb pattern.

Once the spider web is complete, you can hang them up as fun decor for the home. They make ideal window or Halloween tree ornaments with an addition of a loop of string or ribbon. Spook any guests coming to trick or treat with these hanging in the front porch.

Note: This post may contain affiliate links for which I can be compensated.

How to Make a Perler Bead Spider Web Pattern: Ideal Halloween Craft

Perler bead spider webs are best made from one solid color. I've made loads of these webs and the best ones, if you want them for Halloween, are made from solid colors such as black, bright pumpkin orange and monster green.

For a different look, you could also make these cobweb designs out of clear beads which would give a more realistic effect. Examine the pictures below along with the text to be sure of the instructions.

Hexagonal, 6 Sided Fused Bead Boards are Best for Spiderwebs

Spider webs or cobwebs (which are abandoned webs that spiders no longer use) are best made from hexagonal peg boards. This is because the web shape is much easier to make using a hexagonal Perler bead board and they look better too.

I use the small hexagon peg boards. You can also get large peg boards and apply the exact same method with those too so you make even bigger designs.

Step 1: Building the Structure of the Web

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Whether you use a large or a small hexagonal peg board, you will find it so much easier if you place it in front of you with one of the pointed corners in the middle. This is very important and I suggest you do position the board as it is shown in the image of Step 1.

Start by making a complete straight line of your choice of fused beads (Perler, Hama or other) from the most bottom point in the corner, right the way up to the top. This makes a straight, vertical line right through the middle of the pegboard.

Next, add in 2 diagonal lines in a cross shape. Start from the top right corner and make a line of beads down to the bottom left corner.

Then start from the top left corner and make a straight line down to the bottom right corner. Your pattern should then look like the image shown here in step 1.

Step 2: Adding the First Circle of Beads

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Weave in the 'Threads' with the Beads

Now the structure of the spiderweb pattern is in place, you will see a basic star pattern with 6 long branches. This branch design forms the basic building block upon which you can weave in your web threads with the Perler beads.

I like to make two almost circular patterns over the top to fill in the web design but you could make more of a spiral design or something a bit different. If you're using a large hexagon pegboard then you do have more room to be creative with it all.

Starting from the 4th row up from the bottom of a small board, work your chosen color of fused beads all around in a circular design as shown. With a larger board, you will choose where to place the circular sections.

Step 3: Adding the Final Piece to the Cobweb

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Add a Second 'Circle' of Beads to Complete Your Design

Starting from the 2nd row up on a small pegboard, add in the beads all around the design in a circular motion. That means you stick to that row all the way around the pattern. You can see from my image that this completes the spiderweb design.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE Perler Bead Halloween Patterns

These spider webs can be a little difficult to iron since they consist of lots of areas with just 1 bead. You need to be sure that the beads are properly fused together when an adult irons them.

To make this easier, you can fill in all the empty pegs with some clear or transparent beads which will not detract from your design (especially with a strong color like black) and will make it easier to iron.

Another Idea for Your Fused Bead Spider Webs

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

What About Halloween Themed Cupcake Toppers?

The cupcake image here shows one of my chocolate spiderweb toppers that I have used to decorate my cupcakes for the Halloween season. Making these chocolate toppers can be fiddly and time-consuming.

You can use your completed Perler bead spiderwebs made on a small hexagon pegboard to create exactly the same effect. I tested the size against a standard cupcake and it is perfect.

Just use the wet frosting or icing on top of a cupcake to keep the completed Perler pattern in place. Of course you can easily use them for hanging ornaments too by adding a loop of string or ribbon.

Some Completed Spiderweb Perler Designs in Halloween Colors

Image Credit: photo belongs to the author.

Kids and adults who love spiders can enjoy this craft at any time of the year. Making a web from clear or light color glitter Perler beads would look really nice. It can be hung up as a window ornament where any glitter bits would catch the light.

title: Hairy Hobbit Feet Cookies for Halloween
h1: Hairy Hobbit Feet Cookies for Halloween
description: Make hairy Hobbit feet cookies for Halloween: vanilla sugar cookies with chocolate hair, a fun baking project for Lord of the Rings fans.
author: M. W. Johnstone
body:
Discover how you can make some deliciously hairy Hobbit feet cookies for Halloween. Novelty vanilla sugar cookies with chocolate hair are a fun project for Lord of the Rings fans to bake and eat.

Hobbit feet cookies, which luckily have a delicious fragrance of chocolate and vanilla instead of feet, are a really fun baking project. Easy to do, make some foot shaped vanilla biscuits or cookies and add on some melted chocolate icing. Using a foot shaped cookie cutter makes this nice and simple.

You'll find step-by-step photos on this page which show you exactly how to make some feet that you'd expect to see on Bilbo or Frodo Baggins. Perfect little sweet treats for kids birthday parties, Hobbit themed Halloween events and more.

Note: This post may contain affiliate links for which I can be compensated.

Hairy Hobbit Feet Cookies are Ideal Treats for Halloween and Fantasy Parties

Just below is the recipe with step by step photos for the Hobbit foot cookies. Made from simple vanilla sugar cookie dough and decorated with a little chocolate, they're actually feet that you won't mind eating at all - nibble away!

Hobbits as described by Tolkien in The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings books walk about with bare feet which have toughened skin on the soles and they are hairy too.

The hair is thick and curly and will normally match the color of the Hobbits own hair. What great fun these cookies will be for a Hobbit themed birthday, Halloween party or other event.

How to Make Hobbit Feet Cookies

You Need a Foot Shaped Cookie Cutter for This Project

Foot Shape Cookie Cutter, MetalView on AmazonDexam Tinplate Feet Cookie Cutters, Set of 3View on Amazon

Hobbit feet that are tasty treats with vanilla cookie feet and yummy chocolate decoration.

Prep time 30 min  -  Total time 60 min

Ingredients for approx 20 small servings

113g unsalted butter
113g caster sugar
1 beaten egg
1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
225g plain flour

150g bar baking chocolate for decorating
Foot shaped cookie cutter

For sugar cookie dough US measurements, search for a recipe on AllRecipes.com or use your own cookie dough recipe.

Step 1: Make the Vanilla Sugar Cookie Dough

Add softened butter and sugar into a large mixing bowl. You can combine the ingredients with a hand whisk or an electric whisk which is easier. Add in the vanilla extract and 1 egg. Whisk together until everything is combined well.

Gradually add your flour to the bowl and whisk until you have a very crumbly mixture. Use clean hands to squeeze the mixture into a big ball of firm cookie dough. Wrap this ball in some plastic food wrap and place in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.

Step 2: Cut out and Bake the Hobbit Feet Cookies

When the cookie dough has been chilled, take it out of the food wrap and roll it out onto a large, flat work surface. You might only be able to roll a portion, like half of the dough if you don't have a large enough work area. Roll to the thickness you like which is around 5mm for me.

Use your foot cookie cutter to cut out as many cookie feet as you can. Place the cut feet onto a lightly floured baking tray with a small gap in between each one.

⭐ NOTE: If you want to make pairs of feet, you'll have to turn some of the cookie feet upside down so you have both a left and a right foot.

Bake on Gas 4 (350°F / 177°C) for around 10-12 mins. When the feet are ready, they'll be a nice golden brown. Place onto cooling racks to cool down.

Step 3: Prepare Your Chocolate

Take about one-third of your baking chocolate bar and grate it using the large cutters on a standard grater. Put the grated chocolate to one side as that becomes the hairy detail on your Hobbit's feet!

Melt the rest of your baking chocolate. Break up the pieces and pop them into a microwaveable pouring jug like the one shown. Microwave the baking chocolate in short 20-30 second bursts (stirring with a spoon in between) until it's all nicely melted.

Step 4: Get Your Icing Equipment Ready

You might have icing bags but I definitely prefer my Kuhn Rikon squirt bottles which you can use to ice with. The main benefit to these bottles is if the melted chocolate starts to harden up again.

You can just take the top off the bottle and pop it back in the microwave to melt it back again while it's still in the bottle. Much easier. It means you can take your time and you don't have to waste any unusable chocolate.

Just pour the melted chocolate from the jug into your icing container.

Step 5: Ice on Some Chocolate Nails

Ice on 5 chocolate nails shapes onto each cookie foot where the toes are. Hold your icing nozzle at an angle so the chocolate doesn't run out too quickly. Practice on a sheet of baking paper first if you find the idea of icing daunting.

Step 6: Ice on the Hobbit Hair

Remember that if you're using a Kuhn icing bottle and the chocolate starts to harden up, you can re-melt it easily. Simply take off the top of the bottle with the metal tip and place the open bottle into your microwave. Zap in short 10 second bursts (checking in between) until it's melted again. Pop the nozzle back on and use.

Now you need to go loopy with your icing and add some rounded loops and squiggles to make a 'hairy' area of chocolate on your hobbit feet cookies. Just do one foot then move to step 7 before the chocolate hardens.

Step 7: Add the Grated Chocolate

Sprinkle your grated chocolate just over the curly hair pattern you've iced onto the cookie foot. Tap off any excess and you're left with a good impression of textured hair. Go back to step 6 and repeat for the rest of your cookie feet.

Step 8: Hairy Hobbit Feet Ready to Eat!

Leave your cookie feet somewhere cool so the chocolate can harden up before you serve them to any Hobbit fans.

Washing up your chocolate coated icing bottle is easy. Just use plenty of warm, soapy water and a bottle brush! This is a fast method for washing out the Kuhn Rikon icing bottles.

title: How to Make a Zombie Cookies Recipe for Halloween
h1: How to Make a Zombie Cookies Recipe for Halloween
description: A zombie cookies recipe for Halloween: gruesome zombie feet cookies with marbled fondant skin and festering sores for spooky themed parties.
author: M. W. Johnstone
body:
Here's some ghoulishly good zombie cookies recipe for Halloween. This easy recipe features gruesome zombie feet with a marbled green and yellow fondant "skin" which is covered in festering sores. Eat the cookie body parts before the zombies come and feast on you.

Zombie cookie feet are a ghastly but very easy to make sweet treat for Halloween and zombie themed parties. The gross looking zombie feet cookies should really get your guests spooked. These are quick and easy to make using a foot shaped cookie cutter.

Luckily the feet taste a whole lot nicer than they look because they're vanilla sugar cookies topped with sweet fondant icing. They're a really fun project for which you use ready to roll icing. Assembling the gruesome feet is an easy and fun task.

Note: This post may contain affiliate links for which I can be compensated.

Easy Zombie Cookies Recipe for Halloween: Make These Gruesome Feet and Other Body Parts

If you're hosting a Halloween party or a birthday party that features either zombies or monsters as the theme, here's some truly foul looking zombie feet cookies which are perfect for grossing out your guests.

Thankfully the foul looking feet are made with a vanilla sugar cookie base and some easy to roll rolled fondant icing as the topping. They might look gruesome but they really taste divine. And they're lots of fun to make too.

If you have any aspiring child cooks, let them join in by squashing and mixing the green and yellow zombie fondant icing flesh together - it's just like play doh but safe to eat.

How to Make Zombie Body Part Cookies: Directions

Foot Shape Cookie CutterView on AmazonHand Cookie Cutter by R and MView on Amazon

Ghastly zombie body part cookies which look gross but are delicious to eat. I've made feet with shaped cookie cutters but you can easily make hands or other body parts with other cookie cutters. Just make sure you bite into these scabby and rotten feet before they bite into you.

Prep time 30 min  -  Total time 75 min

Sugar cookie ingredients for up to 20 small servings:

113g unsalted butter
113g caster sugar
1 beaten egg
1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
225g plain flour

Or use your own favorite sugar cookie recipe. Try allrecipes.com for recipes with US measurements.

You will also need:

Body part cookie cutters - hands, feet, people cutters
Ready to roll rolled fondant icing
Apricot preserve fruit spread - small amount for adding fondant

Step 1: Make the Zombie Cookie Dough

Place your softened butter and sugar into a big mixing bowl and combine the ingredients with a hand or electric whisk. Add in 1 egg and your vanilla extract and mix everything together. Gradually add the plain flour into the bowl and mix this in as well.

Once everything is well mixed, use your hands to push all the dough mix into a large ball of dough. Cover this in plastic food wrap and chill in the refrigerator for about 30 mins.

Step 2: Cut Out and Bake the Cookies

Roll out the vanilla cookie dough. If you don't have enough work surface to roll the dough in one go, just roll out half to start with. I like quite thin cookies at about 5mm thickness. Whatever size you opt for is pretty much the size they will be once cooked.

Cut out your Zombie cookies with your body part or feet cookie cutters and place them onto lightly floured baking trays. Bake on Gas 4 (350°F / 177°C) for around 10-12 mins. When the cookies are ready, they should be a nice golden brown. Allow the feet to cool down on cooling racks.

Step 3: Making Marbled Fondant Icing for Zombie Like Flesh

I prefer ready to roll rolled fondant icing like Regal-Ice which you can buy in a wide range of colors and it's easy to use. It's pretty much like edible play doh. Great fun for kids and grown ups too.

Ready to roll fondant icing is sticky - to make it easier to work with, prime your work surface and your hands with a generous sprinkling of confectioners' sugar also known as icing sugar.

Take a fist-sized amount of yellow icing and a fist-sized amount of green icing. Push these colors together into a ball and squeeze and shape the ball shape until you get a nice mix of green and yellow.

Roll the fondant out to around 5mm and you should have a great marbled effect of green and yellow fondant. Cut out enough feet to match the amount of cookies that you have.

Step 4: Adding the Fondant to the Cookies

Warm a couple of tablespoons of apricot preserve fruit spread in a small microwave bowl for a short blast of 10 seconds or until just warm.

Spread a small amount of preserve over a foot cookie using a teaspoon. Pick up a yellow and green fondant foot with a blunt knife underneath and place it over the top of the cookie. Press the fondant down gently into place.

Step 5: Making Sharp Yellow Zombie Toenails

Roll out a tiny amount of yellow fondant icing. Use a sharp knife to cut some small triangular shapes out to stick on to your cookies as toenails. To stick these on, just dab a tiny bit of water where you want the toenail to go and press it on.

Step 6: Adding Sore Bloody Scabs to Your Body Part Cookies

You could just leave the zombie feet cookies as they are. Even better is to add on some bloody open sores with a ring of yellow pus around. That is sure to really gross your guests out!

Roll out some yellow fondant. Take a tiny bit of red (about the size of your smallest fingertip) and press into the yellow fondant. Make enough red blobs of fondant for all the cookies you need to decorate. Make sure that you have a nice gap of yellow fondant around each bit of red. Dust a little confectioner's sugar on and roll lightly over the top.

You now have some sores which you can cut out with a knife. Cut out the red bits with a little of yellow surrounding it. Stick these to your feet using a small amount of water.

Step 7: Rotting Black Skin Detail on the Zombie Cookies

Another optional part is to add in some rotting black areas of skin onto your feet. I achieved this look by using a small, clean paintbrush to paint on some black icing from a ready-made squeeze tube.

You could also roll out some very thin lines of black fondant icing and press into your cookies using water to 'glue' them in place. Have fun making some really gross zombie cookies with this recipe - yum!
